title: Pitch Y Combinator
blurb: Ten minutes, one group partner, one shot at the batch. Land on the shipyard office roof.

params.startup: Fogcast: hyperlocal fog forecasts for Ocean Beach surfers

options: Surfing is a $10 billion industry, so if we get just 1% of it we are a $100M company.
12,000 local surfers already pay for surf apps. We win them, then every foggy coast.
Everyone checks the weather daily, so every phone in the world is our market.
rounds.yes: Bottoms-up and specific. That is how we like it.
rounds.no: Top-down TAM math. Every partner here has seen that slide.

rounds.ask: What have you got so far?
options: We're pre-launch, but our waitlist has 4,000 signups from one Hacker News post.
We've spent eight months perfecting the model in stealth so launch is flawless.
340 paying users three weeks after launch, growing 15% a week.
rounds.yes: 15% a week. Keep that up and nothing else matters.
rounds.no: Make something people want, then come back.

options: Two founders who write all the code and surf Ocean Beach every morning.
I'm the business founder. We'll hire a technical cofounder once the round closes.
A dev agency built v1, so we can stay focused on sales and fundraising.
rounds.yes: Technical founders who are their own users. Great sign.
rounds.no: So who writes the code on Monday morning?

title: Pitch Andreessen Horowitz
blurb: Software is eating the world. Convince a16z it is also eating parking.

params.partner: General partner who also hosts a podcast
params.startup: SpotBot: predicts which San Francisco curb will open up next

rounds.ask: Why is this happening now and not ten years ago?
options: Large language models changed everything, and parking is next on the list.
Parking has been painful forever, so the demand for a fix like this has always been there.
Curb sensors, phones and instant payments now all exist, so parking can go online.
rounds.yes: A real why-now. Write that on slide two.
rounds.no: That is not a why-now. That is a vibe.

options: Revenue doubled twice this year and 60% of drivers still use it after 3 months.
Two million downloads in one month, thanks to the free parking giveaway we ran in May.
We're at $1M ARR, nearly all from one enterprise pilot that renews in spring.
rounds.yes: Retention like that is the whole game.
rounds.no: Nice number. Now tell me which part of it survives next quarter.

rounds.ask: Why are you the ones who win this?
options: We have 14 advisors, including two former transit agency heads and a famous angel.
We built parking data systems for five years and know every meter on Valencia.
We're first-time founders, which means we see this with completely fresh eyes.
rounds.yes: Founder-market fit. Love it.
rounds.no: Advisors and fresh eyes are nice. What do you know that others don't?

title: Pitch Founders, Inc.
blurb: Demo a hardware startup on the Fort Mason campus roof. Bring a prototype, not a render.

params.partner: Hardware lab lead with solder on one sleeve
params.startup: BurritoDrop: drone burrito delivery to Dolores Park

options: Anyone who eats burritos, which is basically everyone in San Francisco.
Saturday crowds on the Dolores Park slope, served by four Mission taquerias.
Big chains like Chipotle. We'll license the drone to all of them once it works.
rounds.yes: A beachhead you can fly over. Nice.
rounds.no: Too broad, or too far off. Who is buying in month one?

options: Our simulator says it handles fog and wind better than any drone on the market.
A patent pending on the propeller, plus a letter of intent from a taqueria.
220 test deliveries in a fenced lot, zero spilled salsa.
rounds.yes: Real flights beat real slides. Every time.
rounds.no: We asked if it flies. Paper and simulations don't count.

options: A visionary CEO with two exits, plus a contract hardware shop in Shenzhen for the rest.
Three software engineers. Hardware is just software you can drop, right?
An ex drone racer, a firmware engineer and a burrito obsessive. V1 was built here.
rounds.yes: You already shipped here. That counts.
rounds.no: Hardware is hard. Who is holding the soldering iron?

title: Pitch Founders Fund
blurb: They wanted flying cars. Pitch them something almost as wild in the Presidio.

params.partner: Contrarian partner in a plain black tee
params.startup: Karl Water: nets that turn the fog into drinking water

rounds.ask: What do you believe that almost nobody agrees with?
options: That fog is an untapped water source for coastal cities, and nets make it cheap.
That climate tech is the biggest market of the next decade, and it's still early.
That clean water is a human right, and people will pay a premium for it.
rounds.yes: A real secret. Those are rare.
rounds.no: Everybody already agrees with that.

rounds.ask: Is any of this real yet?
options: A Fortune 500 beverage company said they'd love to pilot it sometime next year.
Our first net on a Sunset rooftop collected 900 liters last month.
Our 3D renders went viral and 10,000 people joined the waitlist overnight.
rounds.yes: Water in a bucket. Now that is a demo.
rounds.no: Interest is not water. Show me a full bucket.

rounds.ask: Why are you the people to build this?
options: We're generalists from top consulting firms. We can learn any industry fast.
We read every fog harvesting paper this year, and we care deeply about water.
One of us designed desalination plants, the other built sails for racing yachts.
rounds.yes: Weird, deep, and exactly right.
rounds.no: Smart and sincere, but where is the edge?

title: Pitch General Catalyst
blurb: Twenty floors up on Hawthorne Street. Sell them on flatter bike routes.

params.partner: Operator turned investor with a standing desk
params.startup: Steepr: e-bike routes that dodge San Francisco's worst hills

options: Bike share fleets pay per ride, since flatter routes mean fewer dead batteries.
Riders see sponsored stops along their route, so local cafes pay us for traffic.
Every rider hates hills, so we'll charge $9.99 a month and most will pay.
rounds.yes: A buyer with a budget and a real pain. Good.
rounds.no: Nobody with a budget feels that pain. Who signs the check?

rounds.ask: How is it going so far?
options: TechCrunch covered our launch and our launch thread got two million views.
Two fleets in pilots, and their battery swaps dropped 18%.
50,000 free downloads. We'll switch on the paid tier once we hit a million.
rounds.yes: A metric your customer already cares about.
rounds.no: Attention and free users are not adoption.

options: Two ex-Google PMs. Neither of us bikes, which gives us truly fresh eyes.
Three of us, equal equity and equal titles, and we'll pick a CEO after the round closes.
A former bike share ops lead and a mapping engineer who rides up Twin Peaks daily.
rounds.yes: You've lived the problem. That shows.
rounds.no: Fresh eyes and shared titles are not a plan. Who knows bikes, and who decides?

title: Pitch Greylock
blurb: Network effects, top of the old phone company tower. Land on the roof, 120 m up.

params.startup: Roomies: a rental marketplace that gets better with every renter

options: Our referral bonus gives every renter $50 for each friend who signs a lease.
Each renter's review improves listings for the next one, and landlords follow.
We have the best brand in rentals, and brand is the strongest moat there is.
rounds.yes: Each user makes it better for the next. That compounds.
rounds.no: Coupons and brand are not a network effect.

options: 70% of new renters arrive through another renter's review, and it rises monthly.
We grew 40% last month, and nearly all of it came from paid Instagram ads.
Signups doubled after we launched a $100 bonus for every new account.
rounds.yes: Organic growth from the product itself. Beautiful.
rounds.no: If you stop paying, does anyone still show up?

options: We work 100-hour weeks. Nobody will outwork this team, period.
We're former landlords, so we know exactly what renters want.
We ran growth at a marketplace and built its review system.
rounds.yes: You've grown a loop before. Do it again.
rounds.no: Hustle and opinions are nice. Have you grown a loop before?

title: Pitch Lightspeed
blurb: Snapchat's first venture investor sits on South Park. Pitch them something fleeting.

params.partner: Consumer partner who answers texts in under a minute
params.startup: Fogpost: photos that vanish when the fog rolls in

options: Gen Z friend groups who want to share moments without a permanent record.
Enterprises that need compliant, auto-expiring photo sharing for their teams.
Everyone with a phone camera, which is more than four billion people.
rounds.yes: Clear audience, clear behavior. Next.
rounds.no: That's not who uses vanishing photos. Who is it really for?

options: We have 50 users, and every one of them is an investor who loves it.
Downloads spiked to 80,000 when an influencer posted about us last week.
11,000 daily users at three campuses, sending 40 photos a day each.
rounds.yes: Daily habit on campus. That is how this starts.
rounds.no: Investors and spikes are not users. Show me a habit.

options: We're still in school and we use it ourselves every day.
We hired a famous advisor who sat on the board of a big social app.
We'll outsource the app so we can stay focused on marketing.
rounds.yes: Users building for users. Classic.
rounds.no: Who is building the thing, though?

title: Pitch 500 Global
blurb: The accelerator that backed thousands. Make yours memorable on Mission Street.

params.partner: Accelerator partner with a growth spreadsheet open
params.startup: Starter Club: a subscription for sourdough starter, shipped fresh

rounds.ask: How do you reach customers cheaply?
options: A big billboard campaign on the 101 so every commuter learns our name.
Every loaf posted online is free marketing, and each jar has a QR code to share.
We'll hire a TikTok agency and go viral. Bread content always performs.
rounds.yes: Built-in sharing. Your customers are your ads.
rounds.no: Billboards are not cheap, and viral is not a plan.

options: We're waiting for the perfect launch moment, probably after the holidays.
Revenue tripled last month, though most of it came from friends and family.
Revenue is up 30% a month for four months. A $9 customer is worth $90 to us.
rounds.yes: Payback in weeks. That is a business.
rounds.no: Friends and family are not a market, and waiting is not a launch.

options: A baker and a growth marketer who have shipped 5,000 jars together.
Just me for now. A cofounder slows decisions down, so I'm going solo.
Four cofounders from our MBA class, with equal shares and equal titles.
rounds.yes: Product plus distribution. Balanced team.
rounds.no: Who bakes, who sells, and who decides?

title: Pitch Initialized
blurb: A seed fund on Tehama Street. Pitch a pothole bounty to former founders.

params.partner: Seed partner who used to be a designer
params.startup: Bump: pays drivers small bounties for verified pothole reports

options: City public works teams. They pay per verified pothole and skip inspection trips.
Drivers. Everyone hates potholes, so they'll pay a monthly fee to report them.
Car companies. They'll license our data someday, probably for self-driving.
rounds.yes: A clear buyer who saves money. Good.
rounds.no: Hating potholes is not a budget. Who saves money?

options: A city employee emailed to say they love it and will pass it along.
We've mapped 3,000 potholes and two cities signed paid pilots.
We redesigned the app twice this quarter. Dark mode just shipped.
rounds.yes: Paid pilots with government is real progress.
rounds.no: Nice emails and dark mode are not contracts.

rounds.ask: How do you two work together?
options: We argue about everything, and that's fine because nobody makes final calls.
We met at a hackathon last Tuesday and instantly knew we were the team.
We built two products together before, and we split decisions by area.
rounds.yes: Cofounders who already shipped together. Low risk.
rounds.no: Cofounder trouble kills more startups than competitors.

title: Pitch Redpoint
blurb: Enterprise software on Maiden Lane. Pitch a bakery inventory tool to a SaaS crowd.

params.partner: SaaS partner who loves a good cohort chart
params.startup: OvenOps: inventory software for neighborhood bakeries

options: Bakeries are a $2 trillion global market, and we only need 1% of it.
Every restaurant on Earth needs inventory software. Bakeries are just step one.
Thousands of independent US bakeries waste money on unsold bread. We start in SF.
rounds.yes: Specific, countable, with a starting point. Good.
rounds.no: Top-down hand waving. Count your actual customers.

rounds.ask: How do customers behave after they sign up?
options: Net revenue retention is 130%: bakeries add locations and seats.
Most cancel after the free trial, but new signups more than make up for it.
We'll track retention once we hit 1,000 customers. Growth comes first.
rounds.yes: Customers paying more every year. That is SaaS gold.
rounds.no: A leaky bucket fills slowly.

options: My uncle owns a bakery, so I've seen the problem up close for years.
One of us ran a 12-location bakery, the other built inventory software.
We're ex-FAANG engineers. Software is software, whatever the industry.
rounds.yes: Deep domain plus technical depth. Strong.
rounds.no: Seen it, or done it? We back the ones who've done it.

title: Pitch Index Ventures
blurb: A European firm a block from a16z. Show them your startup works on two continents.

params.partner: Partner who just flew in from London
params.startup: Lingo Lift: live translation for taxi and rideshare rides

options: Our home zip code first. We'll think about other cities in a few years.
Tourism is a $10 trillion industry, so we're addressing a huge market.
Every tourist city has riders and drivers with no shared language. SF and Lisbon first.
rounds.yes: Global from day one. Our favorite kind.
rounds.no: Too small, or too vague. Where else does this work?

options: Drivers using it get 0.3 more stars on average, and 4,000 pay monthly.
We haven't shown drivers yet. We want the app perfect before they see it.
Riders love the logo, and our app store page converts at 30%.
rounds.yes: A measurable win for the user who pays.
rounds.no: Go ride along with a driver first.

rounds.ask: Can this team build in two countries?
options: We'll figure out Europe later. Our lawyer says it's mostly paperwork.
Founders in both cities who speak six languages, and the app runs in both.
We use translation apps ourselves when traveling, so we get the problem.
rounds.yes: Already operating on two continents. Impressive.
rounds.no: International is hard. Show us you can do it.

title: It's 2010: Pitch at Dogpatch Labs
blurb: Instagram's founders worked on this pier. Pitch a check-in app and find the pivot.

params.partner: Incubator mentor holding a brand new iPhone 4
params.startup: Pierpic: a location check-in app with photos

rounds.ask: Foursquare already owns check-ins. Why you?
options: We'll out-check-in them with more cities, more venues and faster check-ins.
Users skip the check-in and just share photos, so we're cutting all but photos.
We'll add more badges and mayorships. Gamification is what drives retention.
rounds.yes: Do one thing people love. That's a pivot worth making.
rounds.no: More features won't beat the leader.

rounds.ask: What happens after people try it?
options: People love the badges and try every feature once, then they drift off.
Nobody has tried it yet. We're waiting on the App Store review.
Test users post photos every day and keep asking us for filters.
rounds.yes: Users begging for filters is a signal. Ship them.
rounds.no: No pull from users means no product yet.

rounds.ask: Can two people really build this?
options: Yes. One of us does product and design, the other engineering. We ship weekly.
Not yet. We need to hire 40 engineers before the first public launch.
Yes, as long as we outsource the iOS app and the backend to an agency.
rounds.yes: Two people, fast iterations. Go build it.
rounds.no: Small teams win by shipping. Can you?
